A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette:
Marcus

Marcus was nine years old when his stepfather's belt came off. He remembers the sound first-the leather sliding through the loops with a whisper that still lives in his nervous system-and then the weight of it, the particular roughness of that worn fabric against his skin as the man swung it in the dark hallway outside his bedroom. Marcus had woken to shouting, to the smell of alcohol, to the certainty that he had done something wrong, though he could never quite remember what. The blows came in a rhythm that felt endless. His stepfather's voice rose and fell like a tide. When it was over, Marcus lay on the cold floor in the dark, his body trembling, the texture of that belt still burning against his ribs and thighs. The darkness had become a weapon.

Now, at twenty-five, Marcus works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in Portland, a job that keeps him moving through other people's spaces during daylight hours. He is reliably competent-his supervisor notes he is thorough, if quiet-but something has shifted in recent months that no one quite names. When Marcus clocks out at five o'clock, the anxiety begins to climb. Nighttime feels like a trap closing. The dark of evening, the dark of his apartment, the dark of anywhere indoors once the sun sets, triggers a cascade that he has learned to recognize but cannot quite stop. The moment darkness falls, his body floods with the same dread it knew at nine: the sense that something terrible is about to happen, that he is unsafe, that the walls themselves have become dangerous. This is why he has started staying awake into the early morning hours, why he sits in the brightness of diners or twenty-four-hour laundromats, why he has called in sick to shifts that would require him to work the evening turnover. The avoidance has become automatic. When dusk approaches, Marcus simply cannot bring himself to go home.

But staying awake has its own cost. The exhaustion hollows him out, and in that hollow space, the memories return with a vividness that terrifies him. When he closes his eyes-even for a moment-the film plays: the hallway, the sound, the belt, the taste of fear in his mouth. It feels completely real, as though it is happening again, his body seized by the same panic it knew two decades ago. The memory comes not as a story he tells himself but as a sensory storm-the texture of the belt against his skin, the darkness pressing in, the helplessness. When the memory returns, he feels so overwhelmed by the emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing. He has called his sister from the parking lot at work, unable to speak, unable to explain. He has sat on the bathroom floor of his apartment for an hour, simply breathing, waiting for his body to believe it is safe. These episodes are so consuming that Marcus has begun to withdraw from the few relationships he has. He has started making excuses not to see his sister, not to attend his cousin's birthday dinner. The safer choice, he has come to believe, is to be alone-not because he wants solitude, but because he cannot bear the thought of being vulnerable in front of another person. He is certain that if anyone really looked at him, they would see what happened, would see the damage written across him like a scar. He feels like an object, something broken and marked, not like a person anymore.

This sense of being exposed, of carrying his trauma visibly, feeds back into his vigilance. When Marcus is around other people-his coworkers, his neighbors, anyone-he monitors their faces for signs of judgment or disgust. He watches for the moment when they might see him as he sees himself. A child crying in a hallway at the hotel triggers the same fear his stepfather's voice once did; it is not just the sound but what it means, the reminder that harm happens in the dark, in enclosed spaces, behind closed doors where no one can help. He avoids the residential floors when possible, takes a different route through the service corridors. He has become so consumed by the need to prevent harm-to himself, to others-that he is slowly withdrawing from his job, from his life. His supervisor has begun to ask questions. Marcus knows he cannot keep this up. The avoidance that once felt like survival is now suffocating him. He came to his first therapy appointment exhausted, afraid, and desperate for the nighttime to stop being a place where he has to choose between reliving trauma and destroying his own rest.
